title: Indian IT Giants Shift Spending to AI and BFSI as Macro Headwinds Stall Broader Growth
excerpt: With discretionary budgets frozen and overall revenue growth stuck at 3-4%, India's Big Five IT firms are channelling investment into AI-led transformation, banking modernisation and cybersecurity — the few pockets where client spending still flows.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's top IT firms expect only 3-4% revenue growth in FY27 amid macroeconomic challenges.
  • BFSI sector shows resilience with 1-7.5% revenue growth as banks invest in AI and modernization.
  • AI investments are rising, but traditional IT services face 2-3.5% revenue deflation due to AI efficiency.
  • The Big Five IT firms have spent over $5 billion on acquisitions since April 2025 to enhance capabilities.
  • India's top five IT companies — TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra — are expected to post muted revenue growth of just 3-4% in FY27, with analysts warning of possible guidance cuts after Q1 results.
  • Banking and financial services (BFSI) is the standout vertical, with four of the Big Five reporting revenue growth of 1-7.5% in the segment as banks prioritise AI-driven productivity and core modernisation.
  • Enterprises continue to invest in AI-led transformation, legacy application modernisation, data engineering, cloud adoption and cybersecurity — even as discretionary IT budgets remain largely frozen.
  • AI itself is a double-edged sword: it drives new project wins but also threatens 2-3.5% annual revenue deflation for traditional IT services, according to Kotak Institutional Equities.

Q1 FY27: A Soft Start for India's IT Heavyweights

India's largest IT services firms are reporting results for the June quarter against a backdrop of stubborn macroeconomic uncertainty, geopolitical tension in West Asia, and the accelerating disruption of artificial intelligence. The picture emerging is one of selective resilience rather than broad-based recovery.

Wipro, the first of the Big Five to report Q1 FY27 numbers, missed revenue expectations with ₹244.79 billion ($2.54 billion), while net profit rose a tepid 0.6% to ₹33.52 billion. Total deal wins fell sharply to $3.37 billion from $5 billion a year earlier, according to Reuters. Its Americas business declined on healthcare spending cuts and client-specific headwinds. TCS, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra beat quarterly revenue expectations, helped by a depreciating rupee and pockets of strength in banking and energy.

Infosys, which reports on July 23, is projected to deliver around 2-2.2% sequential constant-currency revenue growth, with much of that boost coming from acquisitions — including a two-month contribution from Optimum Healthcare IT and Stratus, according to brokerage estimates compiled by The Hindu BusinessLine.

Where the Money Is Flowing

Across the sector, a clear pattern is emerging: clients are not expanding their overall IT budgets, but they are reallocating money towards a handful of priorities.

"Enterprise technology spending is expected to remain measured during the June quarter as global macroeconomic uncertainty, geopolitical developments and a continued focus on AI-led productivity gains keep discretionary IT investments under pressure."

— Equirus Securities, Q1 FY27 Outlook Report

"Both Infosys and HCLTech flagged 2-3% revenue deflation from AI in FY27 during post-earnings calls in April."

Banking and financial services has been the standout vertical. BFSI revenue for TCS, HCLTech, Infosys and Tech Mahindra grew between 1% and 7.5% year-on-year in FY26, reversing the decline seen the previous year, according to data reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. Banks are prioritising core modernisation and AI-driven productivity, making the segment relatively recession-proof.

"Unlike other verticals, banks and financial institutions are using AI and technology investments for core productivity gains rather than discretionary innovation spending, making the segment relatively resilient even during periods of macro stress," said Vivek Ramji Iyer, Partner and Financial Services Risk Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat.

Energy, Utilities and Resources (EURS) is another pocket of relative strength, particularly for Infosys, which has expanded its consulting capabilities in the vertical through targeted acquisitions in Australia and New Zealand. Telecom and manufacturing, by contrast, remain under pressure — with the ramp-down of Infosys's Daimler contract and weakness at European automakers weighing on both segments.

AI: Revenue Driver and Disruptor in One

AI sits at the centre of the spending conversation, but its impact cuts both ways. On one hand, IT firms are winning new mandates for AI-led transformation — legacy application modernisation, data engineering, deploying large and small language models, and implementing cybersecurity guardrails around AI systems. Equirus Securities notes that enterprise AI environments have grown more complex, with organisations running a mix of LLMs, SLMs, frontier and open-source models, and multiple AI agents, increasing the need for system integrators.

On the other hand, AI is compressing what clients are willing to pay for traditional services. Both Infosys and HCLTech flagged 2-3% revenue deflation from AI in FY27 during post-earnings calls in April. Kotak Institutional Equities analysts Kawaljeet Saluja, Sathishkumar S. and Vamshi Krishna warned of AI-led revenue deflation of 3-3.5% annually over the next three years, as AI models improve faster at software tasks than initially expected.

JP Morgan expects AI adoption to progress through three phases — deflation, digestion and reflation — with the drag persisting potentially beyond FY29 before AI services grow large enough to offset it.

The Acquisition Spree

Unable to rely on organic growth alone, India's Big Five have gone on their most acquisitive year. Since April 2025, they have collectively spent more than $5 billion on acquisitions, according to Mint. Key deals in Q1 FY27 include Persistent Systems' acquisition of Nagarro, LTIMindtree's purchase of Randstad's Technology and Consulting Services arm, and Wipro's buyout of Mindsprint.

These deals aim to plug portfolio gaps, expand into underserved geographies — particularly Australia, Japan and the Middle East — and bolster AI-led engineering capabilities. The thrust on inorganic growth is expected to continue through FY27, though analysts warn that any reduction in dividend payouts to fund acquisitions could dent investor sentiment.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the nearly six million people employed in India's IT sector and the millions more in the diaspora connected to it, the spending shift carries direct career implications. The premium is increasingly on AI skills — data engineering, model orchestration, cybersecurity — rather than traditional application maintenance and testing roles. The sector's pivot to BFSI and energy verticals also signals where new job creation is most likely, even as automation thins the workforce in legacy service lines. Indian professionals in the US and UK working in IT services may find their employers restructuring around these same priorities.

Looking Ahead

All eyes now turn to Infosys's July 23 results and the accompanying management commentary. JP Morgan expects Infosys to trim its FY27 constant-currency revenue guidance from 1.5-3.5% to 1-2.5%, while HCLTech could cut its IT services guidance from 1.5-4.5% to 1-3.5%. Wipro has already guided for a 1.5% decline to 0.5% growth in Q2.

Accenture's recent guidance cut — narrowing full-year growth to 3-4% from 3-5% — has set a cautious tone for the entire industry. Its CEO Julie Sweet noted that while clients are spending differently because of AI, overall budgets have not increased.

The immediate outlook is one of consolidation. The sectors where spending flows — BFSI, energy, cybersecurity and AI infrastructure — will likely determine which of India's IT giants emerge from this cycle in the strongest position. The rest of the business will have to wait for macro clarity that, as of mid-2026, remains stubbornly elusive.
